It's historical.

To make a very long story short, a very large number of businesses made their initial large IT investments in the 1980s/90s. Ever hear the phrase "nobody ever got fired for buying an IBM?" That may not be true now, but in 1981, it was pretty close to truth. IBM was already a giant in the mainframe business, which was the backbone of most companies that had IT at the time. Plus, for companies entering the IT market over the course of the 1980s, it was considered a reliable brand that held the lion's share of the business software market.

Although the IBM PC was released with three operating systems available - DOS, CP/M and UCSD Pascal - all the software was for DOS and the other two were priced ridiculously. As such, as the IBM PC rose, DOS rose with it. Our modern x86/x86-64 architecture is the direct linear descendant of the IBM PC, hence legacy BIOS.

Xenix became available as well, but it was very expensive, as were all *nixes back in the day. Keep in mind that not even BSD had been released yet, Microsoft was pretty much the only company to bother trying to port Unix to the IBM PC, and at least with the 8086, it lacked memory protection, which limited its prospects. Plus, it was more persnickity with hardware, and I'm pretty sure some things taken for granted even then were unavailable, in particular graphics. It was good for people who needed it, but people who didn't were unlikely to pay for it, especially since most of the business programs they cared about were on DOS.

So Unix, being better suited for large machines with proper memory protection and multitasking, and also extremely expensive, was relegated to workstations and higher, up to supercomputers, except for a few one-off oddballs like Xenix. As such, businesses, caring more about 'good enough' than 'perfection,' assuming you can call Unix perfect, invested heavily in the IBM PC architecture. Now, something to keep in mind is that backwards compatibility is everything. One reason Itanium sank like a stone was because Intel (for the second or third time) tried to kill off the conventional x86 for another instruction set, claiming it ran "almost" as fast as a real Intel processor "in emulation." Businesses don't like that wriggle-room, especially since it's usually used to cover up for fuckups, and as such they flocked to AMD64 (to Intel's mortification). As such, "better" versions of the DOS/Windows line - Windows NT and OS/2, specifically - did not take over when people were screaming that takeover was inevitable. They just kept going with what they knew, which was DOS and, later, Windows (non-NT). It was backwards compatible, a lot more likely to avoid problems, and all in all, cheaper. Plus they had already invested in custom software, which gets extremely expensive. This is one reason why IE6 is still floating around out there, because a lot of businesses had software that was validated on IE6. Keep in mind that there are still COBOL programs written in the 1960s in production out there. So people weren't going to go jumping off a cliff for "technically superior" if it endangered their existing IT infrastructure. Now, keep in mind, Microsoft wasn't exactly the best at preserving it either, but they did do better at it than anyone else, and it was a known quantity which lowered training/re-training costs, as well.

Linux came along and ate up the lunches in the server space and other markets, but for the reasons just cited, as well as other reasons, businesses generally stuck with what they knew. If they jumped on the Linux bandwagon, sure, the OS would be free, but let's look at, say, the late 90s. If you went with Linux there your desktop software choices would be, at best, so-so for most businesses, without much of a guarantee for a lot of complex data formats. LibreOffice wasn't where it is now, and as I said, even today, "mostly compatible" often isn't good enough, especially when your company has literally millions of documents that use advanced or obscure features from Office. Remember that Office is a platform onto itself, too, so there's custom software on top of that, as well. But, that said, for desktop systems, it just wasn't practical or affordable for an average company.

The server market, the embedded market, other markets - they were more flexible. The people doing the configuration in those markets were better able to adapt to the changes and harness the capabilities for Linux. Random Guy #48538 in a cubicle is probably not going to care one bit about bash's shell scripting features, he cares about being able to file his weekly report in a quick and easy manner. That means Windows, building on the company IT infrastructure that has essentially descended from something written in the 1980s, or earlier, and built to be accessed by IBM PCs. This all happened as the "big iron" providers largely shriveled up and died - mainframes are still important for many types of large businesses, of course, but buying a $30,000 Sun workstation running Solaris just doesn't happen anymore.

Plus, there's another factor to consider - compatibility. The Unix source code massively fragmented, so that there are lots of source code compatible systems and user interface-compatible systems that do not have binary compatibility, all of which have their little tiny quirks in one place or another. Linux has basically eaten the lunch of everyone but the BSD's, and took a major chomp out of a lot of the BSD's. One thing to remember is that for all intents and purposes, Linux IS UNIX, except without the ridiculously massive licensing fees. BSD counts as well, and if anything it's more Unix than Linux is. Unix's ancient reputation was to be massively powerful and go on massively overpowered systems, and where it was available for x86 architectures it was expensive. So picking up a piece of desktop software for a specific Unix wouldn't necessarily get you that far. With all the standard software being for DOS or Windows, it was very hard to justify not only paying a ridiculous premium on the OS, application software, and computer itself, combined with the fact that it probably wouldn't run what a desktop user wanted to run anyway (and if it did, it would probably be inferior software). There were a number of attempts to put out 1980s desktop applications out there, e.g. WordPerfect for Unix, but again, it would only work for a few Unix platforms (or even just one), and they just didn't do all that well in the market. This constrained the incentive to run anything non-Windows even further, since you probably weren't going to convince WordPerfect to fork over their source code for porting unless you had a lot of lawyers involved and were willing to bleed cash from your financial jugular to do it. In some cases this also applied to specialized hardware as well, which may have only had drivers written for it for one platform (namely, Windows). This is one reason you see some really ancient machines in production, because it's all but impossible to successfully transfer the drivers to a more modern Windows, and the company can't afford to replace all the hardware in the factory.

Now of course, the situation is more complicated than that, and every company is different, so these are all generalizations, but this is an overview of some of the more compelling reasons many businesses threw their lot in with DOS, and in turn, Windows. It also helps that during much of this time period Microsoft did not exhibit as many of the bastardly behaviors that earned them their reputation in the mid-90s, which was revived with intent to make up for lost time in the 2010s. So in a lot of way it boils down to investment, budgets, and momentum, but as you can see, businesses have a lot of reasons for it.

But I get where you are aiming at, but with a little willpower, one could make wine a good thing and catch all calls and run everything as if it ran native.

If it took a little willpower, then Wine would not have a huge compatibility database full of software that only runs half-well. Wine has been working on this for the last 20+ years, and will probably never truly be completed. Windows is an incredibly complex piece of software, and the entire knowledge of Microsoft's OS developers put together probably do not know how the entire thing works top to bottom given its sheer mass.

Additionally Wine is more likely to have very subtle problems. Random crashes that make no sense, specific features that just don't work on one specific application, that sort of thing. And in many cases, it needs hardware access, too, which is not so easily achieved on Linux. Often the custom hardware has drivers written only for Windows and the company that produced it doesn't care about Linux, the hardware is a decade or more old and no longer supported, or the company is just flat-out dead.

This is a situation that looks simple on the surface, but you start seeing just how complicated it all is when you start looking deep into the details of trying to make certain you've got every nuance and quirk of the Windows system right in a foreign OS. Honestly, IMO, VirtualBox is more viable, but there are still serious issues that this cannot necessarily address (e.g. hardware).

As one additional note, in some cases, there are other non-technical issues to address. A doctor's office using this for patient records would probably get reamed, because that sort of thing often has to undergo certification to make sure that they're securing patient data properly. Wine is not likely to win any certifications now or in the foreseeable future.

I'm not trying to rain on your enthusiasm, but the simple fact of the matter is that this is something that becomes bafflingly complicated when you take a look at it, even though it looks fairly straightforward when you're looking at it from high up. If it was so simple I suspect many of these problems might be solved. Hopefully one day they will be solved, but for now, they aren't, or at least, aren't solved well enough for most businesses to put into production.
